Templates: template.template.html — the schema vocabulary

Purpose: documents the required/pattern/enum attribute vocabulary that turns an existing <template id="…"> skeleton into a machine-readable schema, and hosts the one generic validator function that reads it
Not a node type: unlike knowledge.template.html or spec.template.html, this file declares no <template id="…"> of its own and nothing conforms to it via data-conforms-to — there are only ever a handful of *.template.html files, hand-authored, never mixed, so the .template.html filename suffix is already sufficient signal that a file follows this convention. Nothing here needs crawler enforcement.
Sibling of: knowledge.template.html, spec.template.html

The vocabulary

Every type's <template id="…"> already contains one empty placeholder element per field, for documentation/copy-paste. Four optional attributes on those placeholders turn that skeleton into a schema, without adding any new wrapper elements:

  • required — boolean attribute (no value). The field must be present with non-empty text. Absent entirely, or present but only whitespace, both fail the same way: "missing or empty".
  • repeatable — boolean attribute. The child may appear more than once, and every occurrence meets the same checks. Without it a second child of that tag fails, which is what a first-match lookup used to swallow: a duplicate title left one copy live and the other unreachable. Paired with required the two cover four cases — at most one, exactly one, zero or more, one or more.
  • pattern — a JS regular expression source, tested against the field's trimmed text content.
  • required, repeatable, pattern and enum are the schema's own words. Any other attribute on a placeholder — root or field — is one the instance must carry, and a value on it is a regular expression the instance's value must match. So <language-rule data-validates="^(all|html|…)$"> makes that attribute required and closes its vocabulary. The cost is that a misspelt schema word becomes a requirement for an attribute of that name, which fails loudly rather than silently.
  • A leading ? on that value marks the attribute optional, and whatever follows is still the pattern. data-back="?" says an instance may carry data-back and puts no constraint on it; data-back="?^(soft|hard)$" says it may carry one and closes the values if it does. Nothing is ambiguous here, because a regular expression cannot begin with ? — it quantifies nothing and throws. Without the marker every declared attribute is mandatory, so a schema could not describe a flag only some instances carry.
  • enum — a whitespace-separated list of the only exact values the field's trimmed text may take.

A field with none of these is optional and free-form: any content is allowed, or the field may be omitted entirely — but if it's present at all, it still can't be empty (present-but-whitespace-only is always rejected, required or not, with "present but empty — omit it instead").

The placeholders a type declares are also the complete list of children it may have. A child of any other name fails as unexpected, whatever it is called. This check used to compare only tags carrying the family prefix, which left every other name unexamined: a <div> and a <blink> both sat on a knowledge node and met nothing.

Two things lived in that gap, and both are load-bearing. 550 <a data-rel> edges, which is the whole structure of the knowledge graph, and 22 <script> elements, which are the substance of every test case and every language rule. Each type now declares what it holds: <a repeatable href=".+" data-rel="^(depends_on|…)$"> on the six knowledge types and the three language ones, and <script required> on a test case, copying the language-rule that already declared its own.

That data-rel pattern lists the relations a document may use, so one declaration both admits an edge and closes the vocabulary. Two edges carrying relations no list named blocked it until both of them became leads_to. Minting a relation now means editing this pattern, which is the cost of the check, and DESIGN.html argues for open-vocabulary links on the other side of it.

A placeholder that declares an attribute of its own is the exception to the empty rule. Such an element holds its meaning in its attributes, so empty content is correct for it: <figure-edge from="a" to="b"></figure-edge> is an edge with no label, and there is nothing missing about it. A placeholder declaring no attributes, such as <knowledge-title required>, still has to carry text.

A placeholder's children are its content model

Nothing used to look inside a field. The walk read textContent for a pattern or an enum and stopped there, so a <b> inside a title flattened into the string and passed unseen. Every field was free-form whether that suited it or not.

A placeholder now says what its interior holds, in one of four ways, read the same at every depth:

  • Nothing declared — text, and no elements at all. This is the default, and it covers 25 fields that already held nothing else, among them knowledge-title and plan-status.
  • markup — any elements. For prose whose shape nobody should fix: knowledge-detail holds paragraphs, lists, headings, a blockquote and a table across 381 instances, and listing those would only need revisiting the next time somebody writes a document slightly differently.
  • Children declared — those tags and no others, each with its own cardinality and order. Between the other two sits a field with a short fixed vocabulary: language-meaning holds links and nothing else, so <a repeatable href=".+"> says so exactly.
  • conforms-to="#id" — the type at that id, in this same template file. A parent then carries its children into validation, which is what a schema could never say before: a <template> reached one level and no further.

Mixed content needs no rule of its own. The walk reads elements, so text sitting between them never meets a check, and a sentence with a link inside it validates as a sentence with a link inside it.

A child carrying its own data-conforms-to stops the recursion, because the crawler finds that child by itself and checking it twice would report every fault twice. That is also what makes conforms-to worth having: plan-task declares its own conformance and needs none of this, while a figure's twelve nodes declare nothing and were never checked at all.

The order of the placeholders is the content model

A template lists its placeholders in an order, and that order binds. An instance writing a field before one the template ranks earlier fails, the same way one missing a required field fails. There is no word to relax this: a document that does not match its declared shape is wrong, and the schema has no reason to negotiate.

Contiguity comes free with it. The cursor reading an instance only moves forward, so by the time a run resumes after some other tag it has already passed that run's placeholder, and the same check catches it. A repeatable child therefore appears as one unbroken run.

What this does not constrain is the order inside a run. Which task comes second is whatever its author chose, and no schema can say otherwise. That split is why cardinality needed one new word and order needed none: order between placeholders is structure, order within a run is content.

Nothing enforced this until every instance already matched. 31 nodes had drifted, all of them knowledge nodes and all in the tail, because adding a field appended it — so a node's field order recorded which flag arrived when. mycelium validate autofix sorted them once, and every family's writer now places a new field where its template puts it. Turning the check on before either of those would have failed documents nobody had touched. 

<template id="knowledge-goal">
  <knowledge-goal>
    <knowledge-title required></knowledge-title>
    <knowledge-confidence required pattern="^(0|[1-9][0-9]?|100)$"></knowledge-confidence>
    <knowledge-status required enum="pending active completed rejected"></knowledge-status>
    <knowledge-prompt></knowledge-prompt>
    <knowledge-detail></knowledge-detail>
    <a repeatable href=".+" data-rel="^(depends_on|blocks|supports|contradicts|alternative_to|leads_to|specifies|elaborates)$"></a>
  </knowledge-goal>
</template>

Every link resolves

A reference is only worth writing if it can be followed. A dead link is worse than no link: it claims a relationship, survives every check, and only fails when a reader tries to use it.

This is the rule CLAUDE.md already states, that a node may only refer to things which exist in this repository, with something behind it for the first time. Nothing enforced it, and a reference into a deleted database sat in one document for two days while the instructions said there were none.

the citation this audit exists to catch, declared in its data-expects

Nothing outside the type

A document whose purpose is to be an instance keeps everything inside its conforming element. Content sitting beside it in <body> is invisible: no field holds it, no query reaches it, and the schema cannot say anything about it, because the schema describes a type's children and this is not one of them.

A document that defines a type is the opposite. This file is mostly prose about templates, and the worked example inside it is incidental to that. So the audit skips any document declaring a <template>, which separates the two without naming a directory.

The generic validator

Given a type's <template> element and a real instance element, reads the vocabulary above straight out of the template's own content and performs the same four checks every hand-written check() function in this project used to write by hand: required-and-non-empty, pattern, enum, and unexpected/empty-optional fields — including one check, unexpected-field rejection, that spec-doc's own old validator never had, applied here uniformly since there's no reason a schema-declared type should differ. A <template>'s children live in .content, a separate inert DocumentFragment — reading a field's attributes goes through templateEl.content, not the template element directly (verified against happy-dom, the DOM engine this project runs on).

Checking order: schema first, hand-written validator second

A type may still declare its own <script data-validates> alongside its <template>, for logic this vocabulary genuinely can't express. When one exists, the crawler runs the generic check above first, then the hand-written one, and a node is only valid if both pass — the hand-written script is additional validation layered on top of the schema, never a replacement for it. None of this project's seven existing types need one any more; see the decision record.

Such a script exports one default function, and so does an audit. The tag already says which type a validator answers for and which audit an audit is, so naming the export again would only repeat it. A command host exports a default for the same reason, so that mycelium validate does not read as mycelium validate validate.

A language rule is the exception, and keeps a named check. It loads through a different path, and check is a word the language family already uses for what a rule carries, so there the name says something instead of repeating the tag above it.
